title: Ghosts on the water
author: Shelley Walia
content_html:
The steamer moves quietly out of the historic Rütli Meadow on Lake Lucerne into waters of an unbelievable turquoise, a colour that can only be imagined. As the wind comes off the Rigi in long clean sweeps and the villages on either shore recede into their Alpine stillness, the noise of the ordinary world falls away. And I begin to palpably feel the presence of silence and the spirit of the great writers who had come to these waters before me.

It’s been many days since I came to its shores. It was not for anything else but a pilgrimage, an act of homage to the writers and musicians who shaped the way I see and hear and think. I came to T.S. Eliot young, as so many of my generation did, and spent years inside The Waste Land, that great broken monument to a civilisation in crisis, assembled from fragments of everything Eliot had loved and mourned: “These fragments I have shored against my ruins.” What I did not fully understand until I stood on the deck of the steamer, with the Alps closing in on all sides, was how much of The Waste Land is Wagnerian, and how deeply Eliot had absorbed the music that was born on these very shores.

The Rhine daughters from Götterdämmerung move through the poem like waterborne ghosts. Wagner, composing those obsessions into music at Tribschen, just a few kilometres along this same shore where I spent some blissful days, had no idea that a young American poet would one day turn them into the defining poem of the modern age. Frisch weht der wind — the fresh wind blows — sounds across Eliot’s opening pages, a fragment of Tristanund Isolde carrying with it all the weight of doomed love and irrecoverable loss. Eliot took Wagner’s obsessions of desire, dissolution, and the yearning for transcendence, and projected them through the traumatised landscape of the 20th century.

Travel by imagination

Just off the shore near Brunnen, the steamer passes a small rocky island called the Schillerstein — Schiller’s Rock — named after Friedrich Schiller, the German poet and dramatist who wrote Wilhelm Tell, that blazing celebration of Swiss freedom and resistance to tyranny. The Swiss adopted his vision as their own national myth, though Schiller never came here. He never crossed this lake, never felt this wind blowing through his hair as I did. He conjured the Rütli meadow, the mountains, the lake itself, entirely from imagination, so ardently that it possessed his very being, and a rock was named for him on waters he never crossed. Imagination, it turns out, is the more reliable form of travel.

They came, these writers and composers and visionaries, not as tourists but as runaways from political tyranny and personal adversity. The overpowering conventions of the societies that had formed them had to be shed. Wagner arrived at Tribschen in exile, banned from his homeland, his great cycle of music dramas still unfinished. Tolstoy came as a young man barely formed, still searching for the moral framework that would consume his later life. Hesse came broken by the First World War, by a collapsing marriage and a nervous crisis that had brought him to the edge of a breakdown. Mary Shelley came at 18, though to Lake Geneva, in the aftermath of personal tragedy. What was common among them was a landscape so overwhelming in its beauty that it demanded an equivalent seriousness in return.

Wagner at Tribschen composed with a fury and a tenderness that coexist nowhere else so starkly as in the Siegfried Idyll, placed as it is on a staircase at dawn for the woman he loved — the epitome of human grandiosity. Schiller, who never left his study, summoned from pure imagination a Switzerland so vivid and so morally alive that it outlasted every political upheaval that followed. Tolstoy, shaken to his core by the indifference of wealthy hotel guests to a street musician playing outside their windows, sat down and wrote of Lucerne with an anger so grief-stricken that A Ballad of Hotel Schweitzerhof became a lasting wound in his mind. And Hesse, walking the hills above the lake day after day, found in the Swiss light a bridge between the European tradition that had formed him and the Eastern philosophy toward which his broken spirit was reaching.

Solemnity and honesty

The lake asked the same thing of each of them: solemnity and honesty. Sitting on the upper deck of the ferry, as Rütli recedes, the cool wind off the Rigi touches something in me too. The villages pass in their stillness, and the ghosts arrive together with Eliot carrying Wagner, Wagner haunting Eliot, Schiller’s rock rising from the water though its namesake never touched it.

What was first imagined on these waters indeed becomes a palpable experience of what I have so much loved and believed in all my life. To my mind, this is what a pilgrimage feels like. Not the arrival at a shrine, but the crossing, the in-between suspension over turquoise water, in the company of the dead who remain so stubbornly alive.

title: When convenience becomes dependence
author: Priyan R. Naik
content_html:
There was a bandh recently, and I was confronted with a problem of considerable importance: my college wanted me to work online. Normally, this would require effort in cognitive thinking. But instead of exercising my perfectly serviceable brain, I turned to Grok asking it to give me reasons for not working online. It obliged and I had a convincing list involving connectivity, productivity, safety and the general difficulty of conducting business when the city is observing a bandh. I could have thought through most of these myself. But why bother? The lazy side of my brain revelled in getting someone else to do my thinking for me.

This small episode made me wonder whether we have already started depending on artificial intelligence for the simplest acts of thinking. AI platforms have entered our lives with remarkable speed. We use them to write emails, prepare speeches, plan holidays, suggest restaurants, settle arguments, summarise books and explain things we could probably have understood if we had spent another five minutes thinking about them. We even ask them to compose replies to messages when we know perfectly well what we want to say but cannot be bothered to find the right words. The machine has become our researcher, secretary, travel agent, editor and sounding board.

Inherently, there seems to be nothing wrong with this. AI is an extraordinary tool, and refusing to use it would perhaps be like refusing to use a calculator because our grandparents did mental arithmetic. AI saves time, improves productivity and gives us access to information and expertise, once difficult to obtain. The problem begins when convenience becomes dependence and assistance becomes substitution.

Albert Einstein famously said, “The important thing is not to stop questioning.” That may be particularly relevant in an age when machines are becoming extraordinarily good at supplying answers. The danger is not that AI will answer our questions; it is that we have already stopped asking ourselves questions in the first place. Instead of thinking through a problem, we type it in a box. Instead of forming an opinion, we ask for one. Instead of trying to recall something, we Google it. Instead of making a decision, we ask a machine to give us the pros and cons and then quietly select the option we had always wanted.

There is a slightly embarrassing side to this new phenomena. We often use AI not to discover what we should do, but to justify what we have already decided to do. On the bandh day, I had already made up my mind not to work. What I wanted was not wisdom but logical reasons. I wanted my laziness dressed up as rational decision-making. AI obliged happily, presenting a well-argued case for doing nothing.

The concern is that thinking is becoming a neglected habit. Our brains need exercise, remembering a name, calculating without a calculator, finding our way without constantly consulting a map, writing a paragraph without asking AI to improve it and making a decision without seeking differing opinions are all minuscule mental exercises. They probably look insignificant, but collectively they keep the mind alert. If every little intellectual inconvenience is outsourced, we should not be surprised to find our cognitive muscles have gone to seed.

Its much too late to abandon AI, but we should use it intelligently, which means being fully aware when not to use it. Maybe we should first think out the reasons ourselves and then ask AI to challenge them. We could write a paragraph before asking the machine to polish it. We should attempt to recall something before reaching for the search bar. We should make up our own minds and not have AI do the decision-making for us.

Technology should make our lives easier, not make our brains redundant. If we are not careful, we will soon end up with bots that can write, calculate, remember, analyse and make decisions better than we can, while we sit before a screen wondering what prompt to use next. That would be a remarkable achievement for artificial intelligence but unfortunate for our cognitive ability.

title: Mindfulness in the mountains
author: Abhishek Pant
content_html:
When we think of mindfulness, we usually imagine a person sitting cross-legged on the ground, hands cupped, eyes closed in deep concentration. But what if there were other, more active ways to achieve it? A few years ago, while trekking in the Himalayas, I had an unlikely encounter with mindfulness, in a most unexpected setting.

I, along with my group, had ascended the Buran mountain pass, at an altitude of 15,000 feet. The high of scaling the pass was short-lived when we saw the route we would need to take for the descent. It was a snow-covered path, with just enough width to accommodate one human. A towering mountain hugged it on one side. On the other side was a near-vertical drop of several thousand feet – a blanket of snow waiting to wrap around any hapless soul unlucky enough to fall below. Stunned, I gulped at the sight as I began my descent.

Perfect awareness often eludes us. But here, confronted by mortality, mindfulness became my default state of mind. Gone were the intrusive thoughts I had just a minute ago. Only the next step mattered. I was intensely aware of my surroundings and my body. The rhythmic heaving of my chest with every breath, the firm grip of my hands on my trekking pole, the ripple of my leg muscles on every step, the feel of the snow beneath my feet – I could sense it all. It felt as if I had been endowed with a superpower!

The path that had felt so narrow now felt just a little bit wider. Inhale, scout the surroundings, probe the ground in front with the trekking pole, take the next step and repeat. This became my rhythm. With no voices in my head, I felt a clarity that I wasn’t used to. All my senses were engaged. The white and grey mountains surrounding me had never looked so majestic. The mountain air had never felt so crisp. The whisper of the breeze had never felt so soothing. The Himalayan spring water had never tasted so sweet. Every step I took made me feel connected with the ground in a way I had not felt before. I was one with the mountains!

After two hours, we had completed the tricky descent and reached a well-marked path. Although relieved, I also felt a tinge of sadness, for I knew the superpower that had taken hold of me would now ebb. It had been the most alive two hours of my life. I turned around to look at the descent. The sight would be permanently etched in my mind. My thoughts, which had been so clear during the descent, now raced, buzzing with the possibility of harnessing the mindfulness state in other pursuits.

Five years on, as I look back on the descent, I can still recall every detail vividly, as if it happened yesterday. One of my favorite authors, Jim Corbett, was once asked how he was able to recall his famous hunts without having the aid of a diary. To this, he replied, “If one uses one’s senses as they were intended to be used, there is no need to make notes, for everything one sees or hears is photographed on one’s memory, and is there for all time.” Having read his books since I was a little kid, I’m happy I can finally relate to this thought!

title: Longevity without an expiry date
author: Thomas Paul
content_html:
While reading through Scott Fitzgerald’s book Tender is the Night (published in 1934, and hailed as a modern classic) I came upon this authorial comment on page 222: ‘How did he die? Of old age — he was seventy-five. He had lived a longtime’. I paused in surprise at this age-punitive comment.

Had this been a dialogue between characters, it could have been excusable fiction, but it was Fitzgerald’s direct authorial comment about people living long enough. My 70-year-old hackles rose as I read this. I Googled and found that in 1934, the average life expectancy in the United States was about 59 for men and 63 for women. So, grudgingly, I understood where Fitzgerald was coming from. Placing his comment in perspective, it seems that one cannot think other than in the fashion of the times one lives in. It is the social conditioning, out of which it is difficult to escape.

On second thoughts, one does come across comments like this even today — even in the light of improved life expectancy. ‘Ageing gracefully’ is the catch-phrase that has been around for some time, having us all blinking in slow-motion. Contrast this with the poet Dylan Thomas’ revolutionary words in 1951: ‘Do not go gentle into that good night. Rage, rage against the dying of the light.’ Dylan’s was a call to everyone to continue the fight against physical decline aggressively, putting up a fight.

It depends on us to take the call. As for me, Fitzgerald comes down several notches in my esteem, when he caps human life at 75. Perhaps his was the era of surrender to the attrition of ageing. Fitzgerald wasn’t just writing fiction — he was issuing a psychological ceiling, a cap that generations absorbed like gospel. The trouble is, caps are contagious. Once someone says “this is the limit”, society obediently paints a finish line, hangs up a banner, and starts handing out medals for “senior citizenship”. The scary part is that such a surrender is current fashion where social media is abuzz with copy-paste excuses and justification of inaction — a slippery slope where it is all too easy to give up and blame gravity. But here’s the truth: the human body didn’t sign any terminal contract. The cap is in our heads, not in our cells.

We’ve treated age 75 as if it were the warranty period on a refrigerator. Past that, people like Fitzgerald whisper: “He’s lived long enough.” The psychological cap makes us believe that every extra year is borrowed time, when in fact it’s earned time. There is no cosmic official stamping passports: “Sorry sir, you’ve crossed 75, please proceed to the departure lounge.”

Science keeps extending the perceived limits. Centenarians are no longer freak exhibits; they are walking proof that the cap was a fiction. The idea of progress of senility too needs to change. The fervour to maintain fitness at all ages needs a lot of self-motivation. Even if one has never exercised or worked out a physical regimen, that inertia can be overcome. The key is to start gradually. Tai-chi and Pranayama will do for now. Gradual reduction or even elimination of sugar intake is goal two. Sugar may be sweet, but so is the thrill of tying your own shoelaces at 90. The next is resistance training. It preserves your independence and self-worth. The dignity of going to the toilet unassisted is irreplaceable and brooks no compromise.

Our muscles work to the rule of ‘Use it or lose it.’ If you don’t use a muscle group, the body gets the indication that the unused muscle group can be more or less discontinued. ‘Sarcopenia’, the fancy name for muscle loss due to poor nutrition and lack of exercise, is very real and anyone above age 40 cannot afford to ignore it.

The last outpost of human dignity is good health. Its maintenance is low-cost and provides good dividends for the efforts put in. So, if 75 was the warranty period, consider resistance training the extended service plan — because nobody wants to be recalled to the factory before their encore.

title: Speed-breakers are a necessary evil
author: Aakash Bajpai
content_html:
Every evening, when I go for a walk, I face motor vehicles encroaching on the footpath at specific spots. These spots have speed-breakers. Drivers prefer to avoid them as it is convenient to go on the footpath. Occasionally, some motorcyclists even honk at me to move aside and let them pass while I am on the footpath.

Everybody dislikes speed-breakers for their own reasons. Motorists do not like them for the discomfort they cause while driving. They cause wear and tear to the vehicles when they are not built to standards. People with health issues and those pregnant see them as devils.

Pedestrians hate them equally for ruining their peaceful walk when the vehicles start crossing over the footpath to avoid the bump. Bicyclists often wish they had a separate lane free of all such nuisances. But speed-breakers are supposed to augment safety. Well, in theory, yes. Practically, it is somewhat debatable.

A government response in Parliament presents some data to reflect upon. In the year 2014, as many as 11,008 road accidents occurred due to speed-breakers in which about 3,633 persons were killed and 9,428 injured. A year later, 11,084 road accidents were attributable to speed-breakers, causing 3,409 deaths and injuring 9,764 people.

Empirical studies have found that vehicles consume significantly more fuel if speed-breakers are present because of the deceleration and the acceleration that follows. Apart from the energy and the economic loss, speed-breakers slow down traffic in urban scenarios and increase air pollution.

Speed-breakers might have a utility in certain areas such as parking lots, schools, and hospitals. However, their omnipresence fuels annoyance for sure. Principles of design thinking must be applied to achieve the positives that the speed-breakers are supposed to offer. Instead of making vehicles slow down at regular intervals, make it taxing for vehicles to accelerate in certain circumstances, which is possible through modern technology.

Though one wishes to see them go, the rich history that the speed-breakers carry along with them cannot be ignored. Romans have used such bumps on roads to slow down the horse-driven carriages. A Nobel-winning physicist, Arthur Holly Compton, was bothered by the speeding motorists at his university and thus the modern speed-breakers were invented. A group of researchers were awarded the Ig Nobel Prize for linking pain suffered by some when passing over speed-breakers to the possibility of appendicitis.

Speed-breakers have earned various nicknames around the world. In the U.K., they go by “sleeping police officers” and in New Zealand, they are known as “judder bars”. They honour their inventor when they are called “holly hump”. Today, while researchers are exploring ways of generating energy from speed-breakers, one waits patiently for that invention that serves as a viable alternative to those bumps.

title: Young or old, making a choice is confusing
author: Chanchala Borah
content_html:
A few days ago, a college student contacted me. He assumed I could give him advice because I sound wiser than I actually am. Naturally, I basked in the glory and expected my worldly experience to churn out pearls of wisdom to guide this lost soul towards the right path.

His problem was that with every new article he read, video he watched or piece of news he came across, his aim in life kept changing.

For example, he would read about an inspiring IAS officer and decide that he wanted to become an IAS officer. Then he would get inspired by the quality of the video itself and decide that he wanted to become a content creator. After reading a few articles, he now wanted to become a writer.

He expected advice about whether or not he was overthinking and if there was a way out.

Unfortunately, my first thought was: “Hey, I have the same problem. Do I know what to do?” This was an unfortunate discovery.

The problem with giving advice is that people assume you have solved the problem you are advising them about. Nobody wants to hear career advice from someone who still occasionally stares at job portals, wondering whether the corporate world is really their calling or whether they should abandon everything and open a bakery.

I thought about his problem. He wanted to do everything and nothing at the same time. This sounded ridiculous.

Then I realised most adults are doing the same thing.

We have become better at hiding it. We call the young person’s confusion a lack of direction. We call the older person’s confusion a career transition.

A college student changes his mind every week, and everyone worries about his future. An adult changes career every three years, and everyone calls him dynamic.

The real problem is not that young people have too many interests. The problem is that they have not yet learned the sophisticated adult technique of pretending to have one.

Not stopping at one

We tell young people to follow their passion as though passion is a GPS location. Just follow it. It will lead you somewhere. Nobody tells them that passion can behave like a toddler in a toy shop. Today, it wants to be a doctor. Tomorrow, it wants to be police. The day after that, it wants to be an animator. By Friday, it has watched three videos about artificial intelligence and wants to build a start-up. And then, after seeing a successful director talk about movies for two hours in the morning, it wants to be a filmmaker.

Perhaps what this student really needed was not advice but permission. Permission to not know. Permission to be interested in several things without immediately turning each interest into a career. Permission to admire someone’s life without assuming that you must live it. And perhaps, permission to try things and discover that he doesn’t actually like them.

Because that is how most of us figure things out. We don’t always discover what we want. Sometimes we eliminate what we don’t want. I didn’t tell him any of this immediately.

More confused

I felt slightly guilty that he had come to me expecting wisdom and had instead found another confused person.

Eventually, I replied. I told him that I didn’t think he was necessarily overthinking. He was curious. Curiosity was good. He didn’t have to turn every new interest into a lifelong commitment. I told him to try things. And then I stopped. I had run out of wisdom.

He thanked me. Maybe the advice helped. This was both gratifying and concerning. It meant that I had given useful advice despite not knowing what I was doing. Which may actually be the definition of adulthood. We grow older.

People assume we know what we’re doing. We begin giving advice. And somewhere between advising others to trust the process and follow their dreams, we realise that we are all just making it up. Some of us are more convincing. And some of us write articles about it. Which is apparently enough to make a young person believe we know what we’re talking about.

title: Reclaiming the lost art of paying attention
author: Abhimanyu K. Mishra
content_html:
In the past, we could easily focus while sitting and reading a book, getting lost in a story, or listening to someone without constantly being interrupted by mobile notifications; however, this is becoming a challenge for us today. We live in a culture of distraction where our minds flit about, whether we are in a lecture, in a classroom, in a café, or even at a temple.

The buzz of cell phones interrupt class discussions, students surreptitiously check their phones during lectures, and, often, prayer and rituals turn into a photo opportunity.  In a society where attention is divided, the ability to persevere has become a rare quality.

Every day in my class, I witness how students’ mental habits and the very structure of their thinking have changed to the extent where it is impossible for them to concentrate during an hour-long discussion without looking at their phones. The attention that they need, for instance, to understand either complex arguments or appreciate poetry is now being replaced by their endless appetite for amusement and novelty.

Attention is under attack today, with apps, notifications, and media platforms demanding our time. Our economy has shifted from selling goods to selling our attention to algorithms and advertisers.

Information overload, according to psychologist Herbert Simon, leads to a lack of focus. This was once thought of as a theoretical caution, but it is now a reality: every scroll, ping, short video, and reel conditions the mind to constantly seek stimulation at the expense of introspection.

In his book The Shallows (2010), Nicholas Carr claims that the Internet is rewiring our brains, making us “skimmers”, not “thinkers”; it is substituting the contemplative mind with the restless mind.

Attention has a cognitive function that also promotes morality, empathy, and learning. When we pay attention to a text, a problem, or an idea, we understand its meaning; when we listen to someone intently, we accept them as a valuable person; and when we pay superficial attention, our relationships, learning, and creativity are all impacted.

In the Indian tradition, meditation was a spiritual practice long before the fields of neuroscience and cognitive psychology. Arjuna learns from Krishna in the Bhagavad Gita that although the mind is “restless, turbulent, and stubborn”, it can be subdued with practice and detachment. The Sanskrit term shraddha, which is frequently translated as ‘faith’, actually refers to concentrated attention; to pay attention is to honour someone or something and be totally present.

In yoga tradition, there are two steps, dharana (concentration) and dhyana (meditation), which lead to samadhi, or deep absorption. A mind that is disciplined can maintain focus. In a similar vein, sati or ‘mindfulness’ in Buddhist philosophy refers to ‘right attention’, or the capacity to be fully present in the here and now without interruption.

Long-term immersion, memorisation, and listening were given particular attention in our Gurukul educational system. The mind was trained to handle complexity through this process. However, the modern classroom is increasingly at risk from the digital environment. Students’ incapacity to focus is indicative of the shift in civilisation from contemplation to consumption.

Now, distraction is commonplace. We look at our phones hundreds of times a day, scrolling through them even when we are bored, exhausted, or nervous, creating an increasingly uncomfortable feeling that our thoughts are no longer our own. As noted by Shoshana Zuboff in The Age of Surveillance Capitalism (2018), our behaviour becomes more predictable and profitable as we become more preoccupied online.

Reclaiming the lost art of paying attention is a political and personal act, beginning with small acts like not wearing earphones while walking or refraining from using your phone during study sessions or mealtimes. Paying attention to the world, a leaf, a line of poetry, or a human being is one way to resist the culture of distraction. As poet Mary Oliver states, “Attention is the beginning of devotion.”

These behaviours train the mind to lead a peaceful life. Fragmented consciousness can be treated by meditation, journaling, and slow reading. Students should be taught to read slowly, sit with ambiguity, and listen without interrupting. The reward is not only effective learning but also a profound understanding of life.

When we focus, we regain our humanity. It is the purest form of giving and the most generous act of caring; it is recognising someone’s worth and the significance of a thought. This is referred to as ekagrata in Indian philosophy. The mind that can concentrate sees things as they are, whereas the mind that cannot concentrate never finds peace because it is constantly elsewhere. Is this why our ancestors understood that maintaining focus was not a mere act of clarity but a virtue?

Although we cannot stop technology or go back in time, we can choose how we use it. The future belongs to those who are able to maintain focus in the middle of chaos and frenzy. If being distracted is the disease of our time, then paying attention is the remedy.
